vignette: Tahu is a 45-year-old male from Oceania who works as a chef in a busy restaurant. Divorced and living alone, he initially sought help after experiencing escalating difficulties at work that have compromised his ability to maintain his role effectively. The traumatic event occurred about six months ago when Tahu was leaving work late one evening. As he walked through the parking lot, a shadowy figure approached him from behind, overpowering him before he could react. The attacker dragged Tahu into an alley and raped him. Despite the horror of that moment, Tahu can talk about what happened with relative ease. However, his ability to recall the sequence of events is muddled; he often finds himself unable to piece together the exact chronology of the assault. In the immediate aftermath of the rape, Tahu felt a profound sense of disbelief and confusion. He had always prided himself on his strength and independence, but this event left him feeling vulnerable and helpless. Over time, these feelings deepened into a belief that he was no longer capable of doing the things that once defined him as a chef and a man. Tahu's daily life became increasingly difficult as he struggled to navigate the aftermath of the assault. He found himself pushing away memories before they could be fully recalled, which created a sense of disconnection from his experiences. This mental push-and-pull led to frequent episodes where he would suddenly feel overwhelmed by intrusive thoughts and emotions related to the trauma. His negative appraisals are deeply entrenched: Tahu feels as though his life has been destroyed by this event, and he carries a constant feeling of contamination. These beliefs have seeped into every aspect of his life. At work, he began avoiding interactions with colleagues, particularly women, who reminded him of the trauma. His performance slipped as he found it increasingly difficult to concentrate on tasks that once came naturally. Tahu's preoccupation with contamination led to obsessive cleaning behaviors and an aversion to physical contact. This manifested in the kitchen where his formerly confident and efficient movements became hesitant and awkward. He avoided touching ingredients or utensils, which slowed down his workflow and sometimes resulted in mistakes. His colleagues noticed a significant decline in his performance and began to question whether he was still fit for the job. The cumulative impact of these changes led to more profound occupational consequences. Tahu's chef's assistant started taking on tasks that were once Tahu's responsibility, and there were murmurs among management about his fitness to continue as head chef. These external pressures only intensified his sense of inadequacy and worthlessness. What frightened him most was the realization that he might never fully regain control over his life or his career. The trauma had become a defining feature of who he was, overshadowing all else. Tahu's fear of losing his identity as a chef and his sense of self-worth ultimately drove him to seek help. Tahu came to therapy hoping for a way back to the person he once was-a competent and confident chef who could navigate life with ease. He is eager to regain control over his memories and the narrative of his life, aiming to integrate these experiences without feeling they have destroyed everything he once valued.
